Effects of a coached walking programme on activity

Abstract
We evaluated whether a coached walking programme was associated with daily activity in adults. Forty adults participated in a randomised controlled comparison. Activity was measured for seven days using a wearable sensor. The analysis reports estimates and uncertainty rather than clinical efficacy.

1 Introduction
Physical inactivity is a common research target. Prior studies motivate controlled evaluation of coaching programmes. This study compares coached and self-directed walking while recording adherence and activity.

2 Methods
We recruited 40 adult participants and randomly assigned them to a coached programme or a self-directed programme. We collected step counts for seven days and measured adherence. We implemented analysis code to process the wearable measurements. The protocol describes group allocation, sensor inclusion criteria, missing observations, and the primary comparison. No clinical intervention or identifiable participant record is reported.

Ethics approval was granted by the University Institutional Review Board under protocol IRB-2024-017. All participants provided written informed consent before enrolment.

3 Results
Thirty-eight participants contributed analysable data. The groups had similar adherence. Estimates are presented with confidence intervals, and missing observations are described. The figures aggregate measurements and contain no direct identifiers.

4 Discussion
The observed association is limited to this sample and measurement period. Alternative explanations include adherence differences andshort measurement windows. The findings do not establish population-wide clinical effects.

Data availability: De-identified aggregate data are available in the institutional repository under accession DA-104.
Code availability: The analysis source code is available at the same accession, version 1.0.
Author contributions: All authors designed the study, checked the analysis, and approved the manuscript.
Competing interests: The authors declare no competing interests.
Funding: The study received no external funding.
